# Testing

celld makes three important promises:

- An acknowledged write is durable.
- A cell has one writer at a time. It never has two.
- Code written for Cloudflare Workers and Durable Objects operates the
  same on celld.

We try to break each promise at the layer where a failure shows most
clearly. We test the API contract with differential execution against the
Cloudflare runtime. We check the coordination protocol against an
exhaustively model-checked specification, and we test it with
deterministic simulation. We test the full system with fault injection
on live fleets.

## Conformance: two runtimes, one output

We test the compatibility promise differentially. We run each Workers and
Durable Objects program twice: once on workerd, the runtime binary that
Cloudflare operates in production, and once on celld, on identical bytes.
The two outputs must be equal. This shows two facts at once: the program
is real Cloudflare code, because workerd accepts it, and celld obeys the
contract, because the outputs are equal. A test cannot agree with our own
runtime by accident.

The corpus only grows. When celld gets a new API surface, we add fixtures
for that surface, and the fixtures must give equal output on the two
engines. We also port test suites from workerd itself: the Durable
Objects contract, the web-platform globals, and the upstream Web Platform
Tests. Before a release, we also replay scenarios through the full
`celld` binary in each deployment mode: storage, SQL, alarms, streams,
WebSockets, and lifecycle.

## Specification: exhaustive at small size

The coordination protocol is also specified in TLA+. Heyang Zhou wrote
the specifications against celld v0.1.0, and his model checking found
four bugs and a split-brain that lost an acknowledged write. All are
fixed. None had surfaced in our own review or testing.

Where simulation samples schedules, the checker enumerates them: at a
small configuration it visits every reachable state. The model grants
the implementation a linearizable object store and perfect shared
clocks, so a violation it finds needs no clock skew and no storage
anomaly to occur. The invariants are the first two promises at the top
of this page: one writer for each epoch, and no acknowledged write
lost. The fencing argument itself — that a stale owner's late writes
cannot cost an acknowledged write, because the epoch in the key keeps
its lineage apart — is checked, not asserted.

Every configuration carries a pinned expected verdict, and most of the
verdicts are failures: each failing configuration models a bug the
protocol once had, or a deliberately broken checker, and the model
must produce the counterexample. A configuration that stops failing
has lost its tooth. One tooth had already fallen out when the
specifications arrived; we repaired it.

Some specifications model a proposed protocol before it is built. When
the fence on write acknowledgments was redesigned, the design-stage
check produced an eight-state counterexample against the version it
replaced: a dormant cell resumes at its old epoch while its release is
in flight, acknowledges a write, and the takeover that follows
restores without it. The fix shipped; the counterexample stays as a
pinned failure.

The checker has also removed code: celld once sealed a cell's durable
history at restore, and the verdicts showed the seal defended only the
return of a write that was never acknowledged — an outcome celld does
not promise to prevent — while its permanent cut could turn a
recoverable ordering slip into a permanent loss. The seal is gone.

The specifications are a hand-synced snapshot, deliberately not in
continuous integration: a silently stale gate is worse than none. In
practice their updates have landed in the same changes that moved the
protocol, and a delta ledger records what the model does not yet
describe, including places where the model is weaker than the code
rather than wrong. Simulation remains the per-commit ratchet; the
model is its exhaustive small-configuration complement.

## Simulation: the protocol under adversarial schedules

The dangerous bugs live in the coordination: a crash during an ownership
handoff, a lease renewal that races a takeover, an alarm that fires
against a partially restored cell. These windows are nanoseconds wide and
open rarely, so a test cannot wait for them.

Thus the coordination protocol is a
[pure decision core](https://github.com/denoland/celld/tree/main/crates/logic)
with no I/O of its own: the clock, the randomness, and the object store
are interfaces, and a simulator drives the core. The simulated store
injects latency, compare-and-swap races, and lost responses; the clocks
drift apart; a node can crash at each await point. Scripted adversaries
play the cells: a handler that never returns, a write stream that stops
halfway. V8 stays out of the simulation, because V8 is not deterministic.

A seeded scheduler drives each run, so a failure is not a fluke: the seed
replays it exactly, every time, and we keep the seed until the bug is
dead. We examine each property for safety (two writers in one epoch, a
lost acknowledged write, an expired lease that comes back) and for
liveness (each armed alarm fires, and ownership settles on one node after
a crash). A property must survive tens of thousands of seeds, and the
core protocols have run through millions of different schedules.

Simulation has a known failure mode: the checker that cannot fail. So
we also test the checkers: we run deliberately broken variants of the
protocol against the properties, and the properties must find the damage.
A suite that stays green against a broken protocol is a broken suite.

## Live fleets: what simulation cannot see

Simulation cannot see the real S3 tail latency, the real kernel and
filesystem behavior, or V8 under memory pressure. The third layer is
therefore a permanent fleet lab: standard VMs from standard providers,
and a real bucket. The workloads rotate: chat rooms under many WebSocket
connections, working sets that shift across tens of thousands of cells
(each cell has a unique checksum), deployment cutovers under load, and
runs that fill the nodes to the memory limit. The lab qualifies each
release, and between releases it pushes the density and the fault
coverage further. Each run makes an archived evidence bundle: the
configuration, the verification sweeps, the node journals, the kernel
logs, and the phase timings. We keep a red run with the same care as a
green run, because a failure that the harness caught is a result, not a
retry.

We inject the faults between verification passes. A pass fetches each
cell through different nodes and compares the durable state exactly: the
status, the body, and the full message ledger. Each run therefore has a
clean picture before the fault and after it. A cell can be unavailable
for a short time while its ownership moves, but its committed state must
stay complete, and a live node must serve that state again.

The scenarios attack every seam that we know:

- Stop a node with `SIGKILL` in the middle of a write stream and delete
  its local database, so recovery can only come from the bucket. Every
  acknowledged write comes back, because the output gate held each
  response until the write was durable.
- Freeze an owner node, write to its cells through other nodes, and
  unfreeze it. The node sees that its lease moved and refuses to serve
  the old state, and each write from the other nodes lands exactly one
  time: one epoch has at most one writer.
- Cut a node off from the bucket. It fences itself, because a node that
  cannot replicate must not own cells.
- Throttle the bucket, so it answers each request with a 429. The engine
  slows to the write rate of the store and does not amplify the
  throttle, because a node that knows its replicated position does not
  ask a slow store for extra listings.
- Stop a full host at the provider level in the middle of a workload.
  Its cells move to the other nodes, and the returning host joins again
  with no duplicate residency.

Across every run of every scenario, no acknowledged write was lost and
no committed state was damaged; the verification sweeps show zero body
faults, zero status faults, and zero lost messages.

## A few numbers we trust

Each number includes the condition of its measurement. A number without
its conditions has no value.

- **The epoch fence holds under contention.** Five hundred claimants
  tried at the same time to own the same cells: 5,500 attempts, one
  writer for each epoch, zero violations.
- **A warm resident request is local.** A request to a resident cell does
  zero bucket operations and returns in p50 ~1.1 ms and p99 ~7 ms (a
  fixed-host measurement). Only a cold activation touches object storage.
- **A durable write waits for a durability proof.** A single node proves
  each write through the bucket, so one storage round trip is the minimum
  latency for that write. A fleet of two or more nodes can prove a write
  when each follower holds it on disk, and a follower fsync is much
  faster than a storage round trip: a lab fleet measured about 600 ms for
  a bucket proof and about 25 ms for a fleet proof. The bucket upload
  races every fleet proof and either one proves the write, so a slow
  follower cannot make a write slower than a bucket proof. Concurrent
  writes to one cell join one shared upload, so the throughput of one
  cell is not one round trip for each write.
- **A restore is normal work.** Placement handles the restore of an
  inactive cell as ordinary work, and not as an emergency procedure. The
  measured restore times come from the retired external replicator, so this
  page gives no number until a fleet run measures `celld-ltx`.
- **Ten small nodes held real scale.** A fleet of ten nodes, each with 4
  vCPU and 8 GB, held 10,000 resident cells and 20,000 concurrent
  WebSocket connections. We stopped two of the ten nodes, and the data of
  every cell was available again on another node in ~11 s at the tail
  (with reserve headroom).

## The failure edges we intend to find

We must also know where a policy stops, so we record the edges instead of
tuning them away. The clearest edge is the reserve headroom: a fleet that
is full to its resident limit has no space for the cells of a lost node,
so a failure of more than one node at the limit degrades the service,
and a fleet with headroom does not. We measure both sides of that line,
the good restoration with reserve and the red case without, because this
measurement is part of the work.

If you find an edge that we did not find, tell us: a schedule that breaks
a promise, a fault that we did not inject, a number that you cannot
reproduce. That is exactly the bug report that we want:
[github.com/denoland/celld/issues](https://github.com/denoland/celld/issues).

1: # Cloudflare compatibility
2: 
3: celld implements the Cloudflare Workers APIs that this page links to. The notes
4: list only the celld gaps and differences.
5: 
6: - **Yes** means that celld implements the complete applicable API.
7: - **Partial** means that celld does not implement a listed input, operation, or
8:   behavior.
9: - **No** means that celld does not implement the API.
10: 
11: celld must reject an unsupported configuration or API at deployment or first
12: use. An unsupported feature that does not cause an error is a defect. This page
13: identifies each known exception.
14: 
15: ## Services
16: 
17: | service | status |
18: | --- | --- |
19: | [Workers](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/) | **Partial** |
20: | [Durable Objects](https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/) | **Partial** |
21: | [Static assets](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/static-assets/) | **Yes** |
22: | [Cron Triggers](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/configuration/cron-triggers/) | **Partial** |
23: | [Worker Loader](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/bindings/worker-loader/) | **Partial** |
24: | [KV](https://developers.cloudflare.com/kv/api/) | **Partial** |
25: | [Queues](https://developers.cloudflare.com/queues/configuration/javascript-apis/) | **Partial** |
26: | [D1](https://developers.cloudflare.com/d1/worker-api/d1-database/) | **Partial** |
27: | [Workflows](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workflows/build/workers-api/) | **Partial** |
28: | [R2](https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/workers/workers-api-reference/) | **Partial** |
29: | [Workers AI](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers-ai/) | **No** |
30: | [Vectorize](https://developers.cloudflare.com/vectorize/) | **No** |
31: | [Hyperdrive](https://developers.cloudflare.com/hyperdrive/) | **No** |
32: | [Browser Rendering](https://developers.cloudflare.com/browser-rendering/) | **No** |
33: | [Email Workers](https://developers.cloudflare.com/email-routing/email-workers/) | **No** |
34: | [Python Workers](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/languages/python/) | **No** |
35: 
36: ### [Workers](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/)
37: 
38: **Partial**
39: 
40: - The [runtime API table](#runtime-apis) lists the Worker runtime gaps.
41: - celld does not manage a custom domain or terminate TLS. Terminate TLS in the
42:   ingress proxy.
43: - An experimental Workers AI HTTP adapter is available through
44:   `CELLD_AI_URL`.
45: 
46: ### [Durable Objects](https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/)
47: 
48: **Partial**
49: 
50: - An RPC stub cannot cross an isolate boundary. See [RPC](#rpc).
51: - An outbound WebSocket does not continue after the object moves to another
52:   node.
53: - celld refuses invalid UTF-8 from a SQLite `TEXT` value. Store arbitrary
54:   bytes in a `BLOB`.
55: - `SqlStorage.Cursor.toArray()` gives a celld-specific error when the isolate
56:   is near its V8 heap limit.
57: 
58: ### [Cron Triggers](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/configuration/cron-triggers/)
59: 
60: **Partial**
61: 
62: - celld rejects a descending range such as `SAT-SUN` or `NOV-FEB`.
63: - celld rejects `*` inside a list such as `1,*`.
64: - celld runs one handler for each occurrence across the complete fleet.
65: - After fleet downtime, celld runs the most recent missed occurrence one time.
66: - celld runs one handler at a time for each script. It retries a failed handler
67:   until the next occurrence unless the handler calls `noRetry()`.
68: - A service-binding target cannot run its own Cron Triggers.
69: 
70: ### [Worker Loader](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/bindings/worker-loader/)
71: 
72: **Partial**
73: 
74: - Worker Loader is experimental and requires `CELLD_WORKER_LOADER=LOADER`.
75: - A `globalOutbound` Fetcher is not available.
76: - A loaded Worker cannot receive a capability stub in `env`.
77: - Awaitable and pipelined properties are not available.
78: 
79: ### [KV](https://developers.cloudflare.com/kv/api/)
80: 
81: **Partial**
82: 
83: - celld has no edge cache. `cacheTtl` has no effect, and `cacheStatus` is
84:   `null`.
85: - A value above 1 MiB requires a fleet bucket.
86: - celld stores a separate object when an application writes an identical large
87:   value after a namespace changes owners. The separate object prevents an old
88:   owner from deleting the current value.
89: - celld reads a large-value row from an older release, but it does not reclaim
90:   the legacy object after the row is removed.
91: - A namespace has one writer. Use more namespaces to increase write capacity.
92: - A namespace ID can use the Cloudflare hexadecimal form or another stable
93:   string.
94: 
95: ### [Queues](https://developers.cloudflare.com/queues/configuration/javascript-apis/)
96: 
97: **Partial**
98: 
99: - A queue has one writer. Use more queues to increase write capacity.
100: - A Queue owner accepts two concurrent producer operations. One operation can
101:   run and one operation can wait, so an overload cannot delay Queue alarms.
102:   The owner refuses an additional operation, and the producer can retry it.
103: - A queue can have one consumer script. The consumer cannot also export a
104:   `fetch()` handler.
105: - celld retains a message for four days. You cannot configure this period.

108:   Queue event subscriptions are not available.

116:   bytes in a `BLOB`.

119: 
120: **Partial**
121: 
122: - `create()` replaces a terminal instance that has the same ID. Cloudflare
123:   refuses each duplicate ID.
124: - celld replays `run()` from the start, so code outside a step runs again.
125: - A crash after a step side effect can run the step callback again.
126: - `retention` and `locationHint` are not available.
127: - Non-step work cannot remain pending for more than 60 seconds.
128: - A step result, an event payload, and the workflow parameters each have a
129:   1 MiB limit.
130: - `pause()` stops a queued or waiting instance immediately. It lets an active
131:   step finish, and the status changes from `waitingForPause` to `paused` before
132:   the next step starts.
133: - `resume()` starts a paused instance and cancels a pending pause. A paused
134:   retry, sleep, or event wait keeps its remaining wait duration.

136:   `from` option can select a step by its `name`, `count`, and `type`. The
137:   `count` value defaults to `1`, and the `type` value defaults to `do`.
138: - A selected restart reuses each result before the selected step and reruns
139:   that step and each later step. The runtime rejects a selector that does not
140:   match the execution history.

142: - A sensitive step result and a `ReadableStream` step result are not
143:   available.

146: 
147: **Partial**
148: 
149: - An R2 binding uses the fleet bucket under `r2/<bucket_name>/`.
150: - `ssecKey` is not available.
151: - A conditional write cannot use a streamed body larger than 8 MiB.

153: - A multipart upload cannot resume on another node or after a restart.

156:   change the order of stored parts.

174: | [Performance and timers](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/performance/) | **Partial** |

176: | [Node.js compatibility](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/nodejs/) | **Partial** |

178: | [Cache](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/cache/) | **No** |

182: | [MessageChannel](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/messagechannel/) | **No** |
183: | BroadcastChannel | **No** |

186: 
187: **Partial**

197:

218: 
219: **Partial**
220:

222:   does not support `fetch()`, awaitable properties, or pipelined paths.

227: 
228: **Partial**

242:   response.

265:

280:

### [Workers](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/)

**Partial**

- The [runtime API table](#runtime-apis) lists the Worker runtime gaps.
- celld does not manage a custom domain or terminate TLS. Terminate TLS in the
  ingress proxy.
- An experimental Workers AI HTTP adapter is available through
  `CELLD_AI_URL`.

### [Durable Objects](https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/)

**Partial**

- An RPC stub cannot cross an isolate boundary. See [RPC](#rpc).
- An outbound WebSocket does not continue after the object moves to another
  node.
- celld refuses invalid UTF-8 from a SQLite `TEXT` value. Store arbitrary
  bytes in a `BLOB`.

  is near its V8 heap limit.

### [Cron Triggers](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/configuration/cron-triggers/)

**Partial**

- celld rejects a descending range such as `SAT-SUN` or `NOV-FEB`.
- celld rejects `*` inside a list such as `1,*`.
- celld runs one handler for each occurrence across the complete fleet.

  until the next occurrence unless the handler calls `noRetry()`.
- A service-binding target cannot run its own Cron Triggers.

**Partial**

  owner from deleting the current value.

  the legacy object after the row is removed.

- A namespace ID can use the Cloudflare hexadecimal form or another stable
  string.

in an asset directory, and `.assetsignore` requires Wrangler.

See [Limitations](limitations.md) for the operating-system, networking,
security, pressure, and update boundaries.

78:     /// owner this claim displaces if it applies. `None` for a released or
79:     /// absent record.
80:     pub prior: Option<NodeId>,
81:     /// Ambiguous acquires already reconciled for this claim.
82:     ///
83:     /// An ambiguous compare-and-swap is re-read rather than retried blindly,
84:     /// which is correct — it may have applied. But the re-read leads to
85:     /// another acquire, and if that is ambiguous too the cycle repeats. With
86:     /// no bound a persistently unanswered store turns a request that used to
87:     /// hang into one that spins, which is worse: it burns a slot and an
88:     /// object-store budget forever instead of merely waiting.
89:     pub reconciles: u32,
90: }

92: /// How many times one claim may reconcile an ambiguous acquire before the
93: /// request is failed and the caller left to decide. Small: each pass is a full
94: /// read plus a write, and a store answering ambiguously three times running is
95: /// not about to start answering.
96: pub const MAX_ACQUIRE_RECONCILES: u32 = 3;

98: /// Phases map onto the Durable Objects lifecycle states where Cloudflare has
99: /// a name for them:
100: ///
101: /// - `Resident` is active or idle in memory (states 1-3).
102: /// - `Dormant` is out of memory but still owned by this node, so the cell has
103: ///   not been moved off its host. A dormant cell with surviving hibernatable
104: ///   sockets is *hibernated* (state 4); see [`Core::is_hibernated`].
105: /// - `Inactive` is out of memory and owned by nobody: removed from the host,
106: ///   needing a cold start (state 5, and the initial state of every cell).
107: ///
108: /// Note that celld and Cloudflare use "evict" differently. Cloudflare evicts a
109: /// cell *off its host*, which produces `Inactive`. celld evicts a cell *out of
110: /// memory*, which produces `Dormant`, and shedding is what then publishes it
111: /// unowned.
112: #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
113: pub enum Phase {
114:     Inactive,
115:     /// Cold demand queued behind `max_activations`, before any I/O begins.
116:     WaitingActivation,
117:     ReadingOwner {
118:         op: OpId,
119:     },
120:     ReadingNodeLease {
121:         op: OpId,
122:         owner: OwnerRecord,
123:     },
124:     /// The takeover interlock (lease-fold): the dead owner's folded log
125:     /// state was not sealed, so the executor is recovering its sessions
126:     /// before this cell may claim.
127:     RecoveringOwnerLog {
128:         op: OpId,
129:         owner: OwnerRecord,
130:     },
131:     ReadingCapacity {
132:         op: OpId,
133:         claim: Claim,
134:     },
135:     WaitingCapacity,
136:     Acquiring {
137:         op: OpId,
138:         claim: Claim,
139:     },
140:     ReconcilingAcquire {
141:         op: OpId,
142:         claim: Claim,
143:     },
144:     Restoring {
145:         op: OpId,
146:         spec: RestoreSpec,
147:     },
148:     Starting {
149:         op: OpId,
150:         epoch: Epoch,
151:     },
152:     Publishing {
153:         op: OpId,
154:         epoch: Epoch,
155:     },
156:     /// The runtime remains published and routable while replica durability is
157:     /// being proved. A failed or ambiguous proof returns to `Resident`.
158:     EnsuringDurability {
159:         op: OpId,
160:         epoch: Epoch,
161:     },
162:     Cleaning {
163:         op: OpId,
164:         epoch: Epoch,
165:         cause: StopCause,
166:     },
167:     /// Out of memory, still owned here. Hibernated when sockets survived.
168:     Dormant {
169:         epoch: Epoch,
170:     },
171:     /// The owner record is no longer this node's, and a signed peer request is
172:     /// waiting for a successor to restore and publish the cell.
173:     Adopting {
174:         op: OpId,
175:         released_epoch: Epoch,
176:     },
177:     Resident {
178:         epoch: Epoch,
179:     },
180:     Remote {
181:         node: NodeId,
182:         addr: String,
183:         epoch: Epoch,
184:         peer_protocol: u16,
185:         /// Present only for epoch-zero capacity candidates. It identifies the
186:         /// exact advisory sample a refusal disproved.
187:         capacity_sampled_ms: Option<u64>,
188:     },
189:     Fenced,
190: }

213: /// `/state` and `celld diagnose` publish it.
214: fn phase_name(phase: &Phase) -> &'static str {
215:     match phase {
216:         Phase::Inactive => "inactive",
217:         Phase::WaitingActivation => "waiting_activation",
218:         Phase::ReadingOwner { .. } => "reading_owner",
219:         Phase::ReadingNodeLease { .. } => "reading_node_lease",
220:         Phase::RecoveringOwnerLog { .. } => "recovering_owner_log",
221:         Phase::ReadingCapacity { .. } => "reading_capacity",
222:         Phase::WaitingCapacity => "waiting_capacity",
223:         Phase::Acquiring { .. } => "acquiring",
224:         Phase::ReconcilingAcquire { .. } => "reconciling_acquire",
225:         Phase::Restoring { .. } => "restoring",
226:         Phase::Starting { .. } => "starting",
227:         Phase::Publishing { .. } => "publishing",
228:         Phase::EnsuringDurability { .. } => "ensuring_durability",
229:         Phase::Cleaning {
230:             cause: StopCause::Swap,
231:             ..
232:         } => "swapping",
233:         Phase::Cleaning { .. } => "cleaning",
234:         Phase::Dormant { .. } => "dormant",
235:         Phase::Adopting { .. } => "adopting",
236:         Phase::Resident { .. } => "resident",
237:         Phase::Remote { .. } => "remote",
238:         Phase::Fenced => "fenced",
239:     }
240: }

242: /// What waits behind an output gate.
243: ///
244: /// An output waits to leave on its channel. A fired alarm waits for its own
245: /// settlement, because the core orders the consume-side wake-entry delete from
246: /// the far side of the gate: deleting the entry while the consuming commit is
247: /// still local would lose both the alarm and the record that could revive it.
248: ///
249: /// The two settle differently and that is the whole reason this is an enum: an
250: /// output is released to the shell, an alarm is replayed back into the core. A
251: /// channel cannot express the difference -- an alarm has no request to route
252: /// by and no adapter holding anything for it -- so it is a second kind of
253: /// owner rather than a seventh [`Channel`].
254: #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
255: enum GateOwner {
256:     /// An output withheld until every write it can reveal is proven.
257:     Output(Held),
258:     /// The firing alarm's op, and the observation `fire_alarm` made. Both are
259:     /// replayed into `alarm_finished` when the gate settles.
260:     Alarm {
261:         alarm: OpId,
262:         at_ms: Option<i64>,
263:         covered: bool,
264:     },
265: }

275:     position: u64,
276:     /// Read-only outputs that finished after this write committed but before
277:     /// its durability proof completed. They reveal the same state, so they
278:     /// share the write's verdict -- one proof, one verdict, however many
279:     /// channels are waiting on it.
280:     followers: Vec<Held>,
281: }

304: #[derive(Clone, Debug)]
305: struct Cell {
306:     phase: Phase,
307:     /// The shutdown drain has reserved this resident cell for its next
308:     /// handoff batch. New requests wait for the successor route while work
309:     /// which was already admitted finishes on this runtime.
310:     quiescing: bool,
311:     requests: BTreeSet<RequestId>,
312:     websockets: BTreeMap<WebSocketId, WebSocketKind>,
313:     waiting_for: Option<Activation>,
314:     waiting_activation: Option<ColdStart>,
315:     /// The in-flight release of this cell's ownership record, if any.
316:     releasing: Option<OpId>,
317:     /// Whether the eviction now under way hands this cell to the fleet.
318:     evict_rebalance: bool,
319:     alarm: Option<AlarmState>,
320:     alarm_wake: bool,
321:     /// Startup, rather than a request or alarm, demands this activation.
322:     resume_demand: bool,
323:     /// When this cell's eviction was last refused, if it has been.
324:     ///
325:     /// A cell that cannot prove its replica durable goes back to residency,
326:     /// and being cold is exactly why nobody registered it -- so it settles at
327:     /// the head of the eviction order and is chosen again on the next pass,
328:     /// and the one after. Enough of those and the node has no shed candidate
329:     /// it will ever succeed with. Recording the refusal lets the order prefer
330:     /// cells that have not just failed, while still coming back to them when
331:     /// they are all that is left.
332:     eviction_refused_mono_ms: Option<u64>,
333:     /// The isolate holding this cell's realm. Eviction order reads it: taking
334:     /// an isolate's last cell returns the whole heap, taking one of thirty-two
335:     /// returns a cell record.
336:     isolate: Option<isolate::IsolateId>,
337:     /// The application generation whose isolate holds this cell's realm.
338:     /// Zero until the shell reports a start, and the swap pump reads zero as
339:     /// stale: a cell it cannot place is moved rather than trusted.
340:     generation: u64,
341:     /// This cell is moving to the current generation: quiescing for the
342:     /// swap, stopped, or starting again. Cleared when it publishes, and by
343:     /// any phase change that leaves the swap path.
344:     swapping: bool,
345:     /// A forced swap already cancelled this cell's activity. It asks once.
346:     swap_cancelled: bool,
347:     /// The queue deadline now watching this cell, if it is parked. A timer
348:     /// carrying any other generation has been outlived and expires nothing.
349:     queued_generation: Option<u64>,
350:     /// When this cell last did something, on the remembered monotonic clock.
351:     ///
352:     /// Eviction order is the whole reason this exists. Without it the shed
353:     /// candidate is whichever cell sorts first by id, so a node under
354:     /// sustained pressure evicts its alphabetically-first cell over and over
355:     /// -- restoring and shedding the busiest cell on the node while an idle
356:     /// one further down the alphabet is never touched.
357:     last_used_mono_ms: u64,
358: }

436:     /// should not cost a node its whole lifetime.

438:         spec: NodeLeaseSpec,
439:         generation: u64,

441:     Failed,
442:     Fenced,

486: /// All authoritative coordination state for the first vertical slice.
487: pub struct State {
488:     node: NodeId,
489:     config: Config,
490:     fenced: bool,
491:     /// A shutdown handoff is under way: every resident cell is to be
492:     /// released, pumped at most `max_releases` at a time. Sticky -- a
493:     /// draining node never goes back to serving.
494:     draining: bool,
495:     /// An exact clean predecessor was replaced and its local inventory is
496:     /// being scanned or materialized. Readiness remains false until every
497:     /// discovered cell either publishes or fails closed.
498:     resuming: bool,
499:     resuming_cells: BTreeSet<CellId>,
500:     next_op: OpId,
501:     next_timer_generation: u64,
502:     cells: BTreeMap<CellId, Cell>,
503:     request_cells: BTreeMap<RequestId, CellId>,
504:     /// Local routes handed to the executor but not yet reported complete.
505:     /// These are eviction pins: the adapter may still be running user code.
506:     active_requests: BTreeMap<RequestId, CellId>,
507:     /// Reverse index of `active_requests`: how many active requests target
508:     /// each cell. `is_active` reads it in O(1) where scanning the values was
509:     /// O(active_requests), and `worker_request` calls `is_active` once per
510:     /// resident cell — the product wedged cold-cell activation, the rate
511:     /// falling with the cell count (engine/pathological-load.md).
512:     active_cells: BTreeMap<CellId, usize>,
513:     /// Local write responses withheld by the output gate until their cell is
514:     /// proven durable to the written position, keyed by the durability op. An
515:     /// open gate makes its cell active, so the cell cannot be evicted
516:     /// underneath it; a fence drains these to a failed response so a write is
517:     /// never acknowledged after the node loses authority.
518:     barriers: BTreeMap<OpId, Barrier>,
519:     /// Requests whose activity ended while a write of theirs was still on the
520:     /// output gate. The pin outlives the activity: it keeps the cell from being
521:     /// evicted under the gate, and keeps a later write of the same request able
522:     /// to open one. See `activity_finished`.
523:     gate_pinned: BTreeSet<RequestId>,
524:     /// Last resident selected for top-level Worker execution. Cell IDs are
525:     /// ordered, so this is enough to replay a fair round-robin without shell
526:     /// atomics or registry iteration order leaking into behavior.
527:     worker_cursor: Option<CellId>,
528:     activity: ActivitySnapshot,
529:     activation_waiters: VecDeque<CellId>,
530:     /// Cells holding a complete cold-route admission. Keeping this explicit,
531:     /// instead of inferring it from executor tasks, makes the concurrency bound
532:     /// part of the replayable state machine.
533:     activation_permits: BTreeSet<CellId>,
534:     /// Cells with an eviction in flight -- from the durability proof through
535:     /// the runtime stop. Explicit for the same reason as the activation
536:     /// permits: the bound belongs in the replayable state machine rather than
537:     /// being implied by how many executor tasks happen to exist.
538:     eviction_permits: BTreeSet<CellId>,
539:     /// Cells waiting for a residency slot, in arrival order. FIFO is the
540:     /// whole admission policy: waking every waiter on a release and letting
541:     /// them race is unfair by construction — under sustained eviction a
542:     /// waiter can time out while thousands of slots are freed around it.
543:     /// The queue converts "eventually, probably" into a bound: a waiter with
544:     /// `k` waiters ahead of it is admitted within `k` releases, so no
545:     /// arrival pattern can starve it.
546:     capacity_waiters: VecDeque<CellId>,
547:     /// Requests received as epoch-zero capacity handoffs. Keeping the mode on
548:     /// the request rather than in the HTTP adapter makes the admit/refuse race
549:     /// atomic with every other lifecycle transition.
550:     capacity_requests: BTreeSet<RequestId>,
551:     /// Signed shutdown handoffs that need ownership but not a warm runtime.
552:     /// A real request joining the same acquisition still causes the normal
553:     /// restore, so demand always outranks the lazy handoff optimization.
554:     handoff_requests: BTreeSet<RequestId>,
555:     /// Reservations made against each unchanged advisory sample. Concurrent
556:     /// lookups are applied one event at a time, so projected load cannot pick
557:     /// the same advertised final slot twice by accident.
558:     capacity_reservations: BTreeMap<NodeId, usize>,
559:     capacity_samples: BTreeMap<NodeId, u64>,
560:     /// A refusal disproves exactly one load sample. The node becomes eligible
561:     /// again only after its lease advertises a newer sample.
562:     capacity_rejections: BTreeMap<NodeId, u64>,
563:     /// Live routing authority is shared by every cell owned by the same node.
564:     /// Keeping that cache here makes expiry and invalidation deterministic,
565:     /// rather than an invisible executor optimization.
566:     node_lease_cache: BTreeMap<NodeId, NodeLeaseRecord>,
567:     /// Start/publish effects invalidated by fencing may still commit. Their
568:     /// late completion must trigger compensating cleanup, not be ignored.
569:     retired_runtime_ops: BTreeMap<OpId, (CellId, Epoch)>,
570:     /// Runtime starts which exceeded their request deadline but still own a
571:     /// live executor task. A start cannot be cancelled safely, so the core
572:     /// keeps its phase and operation until the real completion arrives. New
573:     /// callers fail fast instead of starting a duplicate runtime for the same
574:     /// cell and epoch.
575:     timed_out_runtime_starts: BTreeSet<OpId>,
576:     /// The cell each in-flight cell-scoped operation belongs to. Completion
577:     /// events name only the op; this index is what makes resolving one a
578:     /// lookup instead of a walk of every cell.
579:     cell_ops: BTreeMap<OpId, CellId>,
580:     /// How many cells currently occupy capacity, maintained at every phase
581:     /// transition. `has_capacity` asks on every admission and `validate` on
582:     /// every debug event; counting by walking the map priced both by the
583:     /// total cell count rather than the answer.
584:     occupied: usize,
585:     node_authority: NodeAuthority,
586:     /// A NudgeNodeLease arrived while a lease write was already in flight.
587:     /// That write's body was serialized BEFORE the
588:     /// nudge's publish, so it cannot carry it. Drain the flag by renewing
589:     /// again the moment the in-flight write settles into Held.
590:     nudge_pending: bool,
591:     /// The most recent wall-clock instant any event carried. Alarms are wall
592:     /// clock, so judging whether one is imminent needs this rather than the
593:     /// monotonic reading next to it.
594:     now_ms: u64,
595:     /// The most recent monotonic instant any event carried. Not a clock read:
596:     /// the core never asks what time it is, it remembers what it was told, so
597:     /// a handler that was not handed a timestamp can still arm a deadline
598:     /// relative to the event being processed.
599:     now_mono_ms: u64,
600:     /// How far down the current sample asked the node to shed.
601:     ///
602:     /// The walk down runs at eviction speed rather than sample speed: each
603:     /// completed eviction starts the next while residency is still above this
604:     /// floor. Without one it is a cell per sample, so a node fifteen over its
605:     /// watermark refuses work for fifteen sampling periods. Recomputed every
606:     /// sample, so a resource trigger comes down by a proportion of what was
607:     /// last measured rather than aiming at a cell count that means nothing to
608:     /// it.
609:     shed_floor: usize,
610:     /// The cut the current shed floor was set from. A later latched sample
611:     /// compares against this: a completed cut that left the number flat makes
612:     /// another cut futile.
613:     shed_cut: Option<ShedCut>,
614:     /// Which ceilings are latched. Held apart from `shed_reason`, which names
615:     /// only the more serious crossing.
616:     latches: pressure::Latches,
617:     /// The application generation the node serves, as last announced by
618:     /// `Event::GenerationChanged`. Zero before any announcement, when no cell
619:     /// is stale.
620:     current_generation: u64,
621:     /// When the current generation was announced, on the monotonic clock.
622:     /// The maximum age counts from here.
623:     generation_changed_mono_ms: u64,
624:     /// How long a resident cell may stay on an older generation before its
625:     /// swap is forced. Zero forces every stale cell at the announcement.
626:     swap_max_age_ms: u64,
627:     /// The classes whose cells are forced without waiting for the maximum
628:     /// age, from the last announcement.
629:     ///
630:     /// Held against the announcement rather than marked on each cell,
631:     /// because only a resident cell is ever nominated: a mark left a dormant
632:     /// reserved cell -- which is what a reserved cell is whenever it is idle
633:     /// -- carrying a forced flag that nothing could act on, and the core
634:     /// refuses that pair. Eagerness is a property of the class and the
635:     /// adoption, so the pump reads it where it decides, and no cell can hold
636:     /// a swap flag it is not swapping under.
637:     swap_eager_classes: BTreeSet<String>,
638:     /// The shedding latch. celld kept this in the executor, which meant the
639:     /// hysteresis -- the part with actual behaviour -- was the one piece the
640:     /// simulation could not reach. It is carried here so a sample
641:     /// sequence is replayable.
642:     shedding: bool,
643:     /// Whether the last load sample is below every configured low watermark.

714:     /// Authority is the lease's published validity evaluated at ask time on
715:     /// the monotonic clock — not the `Held` variant. A peer treats the record
716:     /// as dead the instant `now_ms` reaches `expires_ms`, so a holder whose
717:     /// lease lapsed must answer `false` here even if `Timer::NodeLeaseFence`
718:     /// has not fired yet: the timer is the liveness backstop that halts the
719:     /// process, never the safety mechanism. A suspended VM's timer fires
720:     /// late, but a request evaluated after resume still refuses. The `<` /
721:     /// `>=` polarity matches the fence timer at `handle_timer`, so the
722:     /// predicate and the timer cannot disagree.
723:     pub fn node_authoritative(&self) -> bool {
724:         if !self.config.require_node_lease {
725:             return !self.fenced;
726:         }
727:         let fresh = |held: &HeldNodeLease| {
728:             self.now_mono_ms.saturating_sub(held.last_ok_mono_ms) < held.spec.ttl_ms
729:         };
730:         match &self.node_authority {
731:             NodeAuthority::Held(held) => fresh(held),
732:             NodeAuthority::Reading { pending, .. } | NodeAuthority::Writing { pending, .. } => {
733:                 pending.prior.as_ref().is_some_and(fresh)
734:             }
735:             _ => false,
736:         }
737:     }

740:     pub fn ready_to_serve(&self) -> bool {
741:         if self.fenced || self.resuming {
742:             return false;
743:         }
744:         self.node_authoritative()
745:     }

859:     /// Return every pin on every resident reserved for a shutdown handoff.
860:     /// A cell without an active request still gets one row, so a regular or
861:     /// outbound WebSocket cannot leave an otherwise empty stall invisible.
862:     pub fn drain_pins(&self) -> Vec<DrainPin> {
863:         let mut pins = Vec::new();
864:         for (cell, state) in self.cells.iter().filter(|(_, cell)| cell.quiescing) {
865:             let active: Vec<RequestId> = self
866:                 .active_requests
867:                 .iter()
868:                 .filter_map(|(request, request_cell)| (request_cell == cell).then_some(*request))
869:                 .collect();
870:             let regular_websocket_count = state
871:                 .websockets
872:                 .values()
873:                 .filter(|kind| matches!(kind, WebSocketKind::Regular))
874:                 .count();
875:             let outbound_websocket_count = state
876:                 .websockets
877:                 .values()
878:                 .filter(|kind| matches!(kind, WebSocketKind::Outbound))
879:                 .count();
880:             if active.is_empty() {
881:                 pins.push(DrainPin {
882:                     cell: cell.clone(),
883:                     request: None,
884:                     active_request_count: 0,
885:                     output_gate_count: 0,
886:                     regular_websocket_count,
887:                     outbound_websocket_count,
888:                 });
889:                 continue;
890:             }
891:             let active_request_count = active.len();
892:             for request in active {
893:                 pins.push(DrainPin {
894:                     cell: cell.clone(),
895:                     request: Some(request),
896:                     active_request_count,
897:                     output_gate_count: self
898:                         .barriers
899:                         .values()
900:                         .filter(|barrier| {
901:                             matches!(&barrier.owner, GateOwner::Output(held) if held.request == request)
902:                                 || barrier.followers.iter().any(|held| held.request == request)
903:                         })
904:                         .count(),
905:                     regular_websocket_count,
906:                     outbound_websocket_count,
907:                 });
908:             }
909:         }
910:         pins
911:     }

970:     /// `occupied` cannot say: it counts residency, so a node holding thousands

999:     /// store, where the write loses a race against a 50ms drain poll that

1045:     /// Cheap internal consistency gate run by both executors after every event.
1046:     /// Check one withheld output: pinned on the barrier's cell, and the only
1047:     /// output this request holds on that channel.
1048:     fn validate_held(
1049:         held: &Held,
1050:         op: &OpId,
1051:         barrier: &Barrier,
1052:         active_requests: &BTreeMap<RequestId, CellId>,
1053:         seen: &mut BTreeSet<(RequestId, &'static str)>,
1054:     ) -> Result<(), String> {
1055:         if active_requests.get(&held.request) != Some(&barrier.cell) {
1056:             return Err(format!(
1057:                 "held output {} on {} behind op {op} is not pinned on {:?}",
1058:                 held.request,
1059:                 held.channel.as_str(),
1060:                 barrier.cell
1061:             ));
1062:         }
1063:         if !seen.insert((held.request, held.channel.as_str())) {
1064:             return Err(format!(
1065:                 "request {} has two outputs held on {}",
1066:                 held.request,
1067:                 held.channel.as_str()
1068:             ));
1069:         }
1070:         Ok(())
1071:     }

1073:     pub fn validate(&self) -> Result<(), String> {
1074:         if !self.occupied_below(self.config.max_resident.saturating_add(1)) {
1075:             return Err(format!(
1076:                 "occupied {} exceeds ceiling {}",
1077:                 self.occupied(),
1078:                 self.config.max_resident
1079:             ));
1080:         }
1081:         let eviction_ceiling = if self.draining {
1082:             self.config.max_releases.max(self.config.max_evictions)
1083:         } else {
1084:             self.config.max_evictions
1085:         };
1086:         if self.eviction_permits.len() > eviction_ceiling {
1087:             return Err(format!(
1088:                 "evicting {} exceeds ceiling {}",
1089:                 self.eviction_permits.len(),
1090:                 eviction_ceiling
1091:             ));
1092:         }
1093:         let handoffs = self
1094:             .quiescing()
1095:             .saturating_add(self.eviction_permits.len())
1096:             .saturating_add(self.releasing())
1097:             .saturating_add(self.adopting());
1098:         if self.draining && handoffs > self.config.max_releases {
1099:             return Err(format!(
1100:                 "handoffs {handoffs} exceeds release ceiling {}",
1101:                 self.config.max_releases
1102:             ));
1103:         }
1104:         if self.activation_permits.len() > self.config.max_activations {
1105:             return Err(format!(
1106:                 "activating {} exceeds ceiling {}",
1107:                 self.activation_permits.len(),
1108:                 self.config.max_activations
1109:             ));
1110:         }
1111: 
1112:         let mut activation_queued = BTreeSet::new();
1113:         for id in &self.activation_waiters {
1114:             if !activation_queued.insert(id) {
1115:                 return Err(format!("activation waiter {id:?} is queued twice"));
1116:             }
1117:             let Some(cell) = self.cells.get(id) else {
1118:                 return Err(format!("activation waiter {id:?} has no cell state"));
1119:             };
1120:             if cell.phase != Phase::WaitingActivation || cell.waiting_activation.is_none() {
1121:                 return Err(format!("activation waiter {id:?} is not waiting"));
1122:             }
1123:             if self.activation_permits.contains(id) {
1124:                 return Err(format!("activation waiter {id:?} also holds a permit"));
1125:             }
1126:         }
1127:         for id in &self.activation_permits {
1128:             let Some(cell) = self.cells.get(id) else {
1129:                 return Err(format!("activation permit {id:?} has no cell state"));
1130:             };
1131:             if !phase_holds_activation(&cell.phase) {
1132:                 return Err(format!(
1133:                     "activation permit {id:?} is held in terminal phase {:?}",
1134:                     cell.phase
1135:                 ));
1136:             }
1137:         }
1138: 
1139:         let mut queued = BTreeSet::new();
1140:         for id in &self.capacity_waiters {
1141:             if !queued.insert(id) {
1142:                 return Err(format!("capacity waiter {id:?} is queued twice"));
1143:             }
1144:             let Some(cell) = self.cells.get(id) else {
1145:                 return Err(format!("capacity waiter {id:?} has no cell state"));
1146:             };
1147:             if cell.phase != Phase::WaitingCapacity || cell.waiting_for.is_none() {
1148:                 return Err(format!("capacity waiter {id:?} is not waiting"));
1149:             }
1150:         }
1151:         for (id, cell) in &self.cells {
1152:             if cell.quiescing && !matches!(cell.phase, Phase::Resident { .. }) {
1153:                 return Err(format!(
1154:                     "cell {id:?} is quiescing in non-resident phase {:?}",
1155:                     cell.phase
1156:                 ));
1157:             }
1158:             if cell.swapping
1159:                 && !matches!(
1160:                     cell.phase,
1161:                     Phase::Resident { .. }
1162:                         | Phase::Cleaning {
1163:                             cause: StopCause::Swap,
1164:                             ..
1165:                         }
1166:                         | Phase::Starting { .. }
1167:                         | Phase::Publishing { .. }
1168:                 )
1169:             {
1170:                 return Err(format!(
1171:                     "cell {id:?} is swapping in phase {:?}, outside the swap path",
1172:                     cell.phase
1173:                 ));
1174:             }
1175:             if cell.swap_cancelled && !cell.swapping {
1176:                 return Err(format!("cell {id:?} carries a swap flag without swapping"));
1177:             }
1178:             let is_activation_queued = activation_queued.contains(id);
1179:             if (cell.phase == Phase::WaitingActivation) != is_activation_queued {
1180:                 return Err(format!("cell {id:?} activation queue and phase disagree"));
1181:             }
1182:             if phase_requires_activation_permit(&cell.phase, cell.swapping)
1183:                 && !self.activation_permits.contains(id)
1184:             {
1185:                 return Err(format!(
1186:                     "cell {id:?} is in activation phase {:?} without a permit",
1187:                     cell.phase
1188:                 ));
1189:             }
1190:             let is_queued = queued.contains(id);
1191:             if (cell.phase == Phase::WaitingCapacity) != is_queued {
1192:                 return Err(format!("cell {id:?} queue and phase disagree"));
1193:             }
1194:             for request in &cell.requests {
1195:                 if self.request_cells.get(request) != Some(id) {
1196:                     return Err(format!(
1197:                         "request {request} index disagrees with cell {id:?}"
1198:                     ));
1199:                 }
1200:             }
1201:             // Every in-flight cell op must be resolvable through the index,
1202:             // or its completion event will never find this cell.
1203:             let indexed = |op: OpId| self.cell_ops.get(&op) == Some(id);
1204:             if let Some(op) = phase_op(&cell.phase) {
1205:                 if !indexed(op) {
1206:                     return Err(format!("cell {id:?} phase op {op} is not indexed"));
1207:                 }
1208:             }
1209:             if let Some(AlarmState::Firing { op, .. }) = cell.alarm {
1210:                 if !indexed(op) {
1211:                     return Err(format!("cell {id:?} firing alarm op {op} is not indexed"));
1212:                 }
1213:             }
1214:             if let Some(op) = cell.releasing {
1215:                 if !indexed(op) {
1216:                     return Err(format!("cell {id:?} release op {op} is not indexed"));
1217:                 }
1218:             }
1219:         }
1220:         let walked = self
1221:             .cells
1222:             .values()
1223:             .filter(|cell| phase_occupies_capacity(&cell.phase))
1224:             .count();
1225:         if walked != self.occupied {
1226:             return Err(format!(
1227:                 "occupied counter {} disagrees with the walk {walked}",
1228:                 self.occupied
1229:             ));
1230:         }
1231:         for (request, id) in &self.request_cells {
1232:             if !self
1233:                 .cells
1234:                 .get(id)

It's a Rust workspace ("celld") for self-hosted distributed Durable Objects - a Cloudflare Workers/Durable Objects-compatible runtime running on operator-owned machines with object storage as the durable backing. pages.title: celld Quickstart
pages.purpose: Practical quickstart covering install, local development with celld dev, deploying an application, and running a fleet node.
instructions: Describe the fastest path from clone to a running Worker.
Cover both local `celld dev` and a Cloud bucket fleet.
List the exact commands for install, deploy, and node start.

pages.title: celld Architecture
pages.purpose: Explain the overall system: the node/fleet model, cells as Durable Objects with per-cell SQLite, the bucket as root of authority, the clean-sheet decision core split between crates/logic and crates/celld, and end-to-end control/data flow.
instructions: Explain the node-fleet-cell model and the bucket ownership mechanism.
Document the clean-sheet boundary: crates/logic is a pure decision core with no I/O; crates/celld is the effect executor.
Trace the actor serialization model and how events and effects flow.
Describe the workspace crate boundary and release build profile choices.

pages.title: Durability, Fencing, and the Replication Protocol
pages.purpose: Document RPO=0 durability guarantees, epoch fencing, ownership records, node-log ensemble replication, the takeover recovery gate, storage requirements, and self-fencing.
instructions: Detail the bucket requirements (conditional writes, read-after-write).
Explain the ownership record, epoch prefix, acknowledgement rule, and the fleet node-log ensemble.
Explain self-fencing and the takeover recovery gate.
Cover the LTX format and celld-ltx replication.

pages.title: V8 Runtime, JS Embedding, and Application Execution
pages.purpose: Describe how celld embeds V8, runs Wrangler workers and Durable Objects, the isolate pool, the Durable Object storage/SQL interface, WebSockets, and worker features like cron, KV, Queues, D1, Workflows, R2, and Assets.
instructions: Document the RuntimeManager lifecycle (start/publish/stop) and the actor lifecycle.
Describe isolate pooling with v8::Locker and the shared Worker queue.
Document the cell storage (per-cell SQLite) and Durable Object storage API.
Describe the reserved cells for D1, KV, Queues, cron, and Workflows.

pages.title: Object Storage Backends and Bucket Contract
pages.purpose: Document the bucket abstraction across S3-compatible, Google Cloud Storage, and Azure Blob Storage: conditional-write dialects, credentials, layout, prefixes, the storage probe, and the fleet key prefix.
instructions: Describe the two conditional-write dialects (S3 etag, GCS generation).
Document credential sources per provider (AWS chain, ADC, Azure families).
Enumerate the reserved bucket prefixes and the storage test.
Explain the fleet key prefix scheme.

pages.title: Cloudflare Compatibility Boundary
pages.purpose: Document the Cloudflare Workers and Durable Objects API surface celld implements, the supported Wrangler configuration subset, deployed services, and known compatibility gaps.
instructions: Catalog implemented vs partial vs unsupported services and APIs.
Document the Wrangler config keys celld accepts and rejects.
Explain the deployment feature gates and manifest schema.
Note silent-stub gaps as known exceptions.

pages.title: Fleet Operations, Diagnostics, and Configuration
pages.purpose: Explain operating a fleet: node leases, graceful shutdown and handoff, fleet readiness, operator CLI subcommands (diagnose, cell list, d1, kv, queue), environment variables, memory pressure, and deployment rollouts.
instructions: Document node leases, drain token, graceful shutdown handoff, and rolling upgrades.
Document the operator CLI subcommands and internal operator API routes.
Explain memory pressure shedding and all the key environment variables.
Document deployment adoption and the first-readiness gate.

pages.title: Testing and Verification Strategy
pages.purpose: Explain celld's multi-layer verification: differential conformance vs workerd, TLA+ model checking, deterministic simulation of the pure decision core, and live fleet fault injection.
instructions: Describe the four verification layers.
Explain the pure-decision-core design that makes simulation possible.
Document the fault-injection scenarios and the numbers the project trusts.

pages.title: Telemetry and Observability
pages.purpose: Describe the optional telemetry system: Parquet-to-bucket sink, OTLP sink, the span/log schema, compaction, DuckDB querying, and configuration.
instructions: Document the bucket and OTLP sinks and all telemetry environment variables.
Explain the event schema and trace correlation.
Cover the Parquet file format, partitioning, compaction, and DuckDB querying.

pages.title: Security Boundary
pages.purpose: Explain celld's security model: the trust boundary, the two listeners, the fleet HMAC peer authentication, the internal operator API authentication, request-body limits, and bucket credential handling.
instructions: Document the trust model (one fleet, one app) and external boundaries.
Explain the public vs internal listener split and the peer tunnel.
Detail the fleet HMAC, clock limit, and replay protection.
Document operator API routes and their authentication.

pages.title: Limitations and Alpha Boundaries
pages.purpose: Document the alpha-era operational limits: single-application fleets, no TLS, plaintext peer traffic, storage credential requirements, WebSocket restrictions, and platform support.
instructions: Catalog the known limitations across fleets, networking, storage credentials, WebSockets, and platforms.
State uncertainty where the repository does not establish a fact.

pages.title: Change Guides for Representative Maintenance Tasks
pages.purpose: Focused, source-grounded guides for common maintenance tasks: changing a protocol/durability decision, adding a new Worker API surface, tuning presconcopic knobs, and operating a rolling upgrade.
instructions: Guide readers to the pure decision core before the effect adapter for any behavior change.
Explain how to add a new Worker API surface conformantly.
Explain how a protocol change must be gated by the peer protocol version.
Point to the simulation, model, and conformance layers that verify a change.

---
type: architecture
title: celld Architecture
description: The node-fleet-cell model, per-cell SQLite, the bucket as root of authority, the clean-sheet decision-core split between crates/logic and crates/celld, and the event-effect control loop.
tags: [architecture, durable-objects, decision-core, actor, bucket]
---

# celld Architecture

celld is a self-hosted, distributed implementation of Cloudflare Workers and
Durable Objects. One `celld` process is a **node**; the nodes that share one
object-storage bucket form a **fleet**; and each Durable Object instance is a
**cell** — a named server with its own private SQLite database. Exactly one
node owns a cell at a time, and the bucket holds the durable authority that
decides who owns what.

The workspace is deliberately split into a pure decision core and an effect
executor. `crates/logic` owns every behavioral decision and has no I/O, clocks,
randomness, or locks. `crates/celld` is the effect executor and V8 host, and
`crates/ltx` provides the in-process SQLite replication format. This split is
declared at the top of the workspace `Cargo.toml`:

> `crates/logic` owns all behavioral state and decisions; `crates/celld` is
> only an effect executor and adapter host.

## The workspace

The root `Cargo.toml` declares three members — `crates/*` — with every direct
dependency pinned once in `[workspace.dependencies]` so the crates can never
drift onto two versions of one crate (`Cargo.toml` lines 3-5, 33-35).

The release profile is size- and speed-tuned with `lto = "fat"`,
`codegen-units = 1`, `opt-level = "s"`, `panic = "abort"`, and `strip = true`
(`Cargo.toml` lines 9-14). A separate `lab` profile ships unsstripped with
`lto = "thin"`, `codegen-units = 16`, `incremental = true`, and line tables so
`perf` can attribute CPU by function during lab runs (`Cargo.toml` lines
19-27). The binary sets the global allocator to jemalloc because glibc's arena
serialization measurably reduced throughput (`crates/celld/main.rs` lines 44-50).

### Crate boundaries

- **`celld-logic`** (`crates/logic`) is a "pure decision core: no async, I/O,
  clocks, randomness, locks, or dependencies" (`crates/logic/Cargo.toml`). Its
  single entrypoint is `on_event`, and no adapter may mutate `State` directly
  (`crates/logic/lib.rs` lines 3-7). The production executor and the
  deterministic simulator both feed it events and perform the effects it
  returns, which is what makes the coordination protocol deterministically
  testable.
- **`celld`** (`crates/celld`) is the executable. It owns the V8 runtime, the
  HTTP and peer listeners, the SQLite files, the object-store client, and the
  serial actor that repeatedly drives `celld_logic::on_event`
  (`crates/celld/lib.rs` lines 7-10).
- **`celld-ltx`** (`crates/ltx`) provides "embeddable streaming replication
  for a SQLite database": it captures WAL data as LTX segments, restores
  databases, compacts levels, and reads bundle objects (`crates/ltx/src/lib.rs`
  lines 1-fp, 9-11). It is a from-scratch Rust reimplementation of the Litestream v0.5
  replication behavior and the LTX v0.5.2 block format, vendored and owned by
  celld rather than tracked against an upstream branch
  (`crates/ltx/Cargo.toml`).

## The node-fleet-cell model

A cell maps onto a Durable Object: "a small server with a name and a private
SQLite database" (`docs/README.md` line 8-9). Each cell runs on one thread; a
second request interleaves only while the first awaits, and storage operations
are synchronous and never interleave, so the data in a cell stays consistent
(`docs/README.md` lines 12-14). Cells share no database.

Cell lifecycle states mirror Durable Objects (`crates/logic/lib.rs` lines
98-111 and `Phase` at lines 113-190):

- **Inactive** — out of memory and owned by nobody; the initial state of every
  cell and "only an object in the bucket, so it costs almost zero".
- **Resident** — in memory, and either **active** (doing work) or **idle**
  (waiting). The runtime removes an idle cell from memory.
- **Hibernated** — a cell removed from memory that keeps its hibernatable
  WebSocket clients and stays on its node.
- **Dormant** — out of memory but still owned by this node.

A cell keeps no memory across these transitions, so its constructor runs again
on the next event (`docs/README.md` lines 30-34).

The data path is per-cell SQLite: "Each cell is its OWN db file (its own
replicated, epoch-fenced bucket prefix)" (`crates/celld/storage.rs` lines
NA-NA). `ctx.storage` is async in JS but synchronous underneath (local SQLite),
and the JS harness wraps synchronous Rust ops in async rather than hoisting a
separate thread (`crates/celld/storage.rs`).

## The bucket as root of authority

The fleet bucket holds "the deployments, the cell state, the ownership records,
the node leases, and the peer-authentication secret" (`docs/security.md`
lines 141-143). Two properties make this the authority:

1. **Conditional writes.** celld claims a cell by writing a small ownership
   record "with a condition the storage enforces — the write succeeds only if
   nobody else changed the record first" (`docs/README.md` lines 40-43). The
   bucket therefore "decides who wins, and two nodes cannot both claim the same
   cell". The claim expires unless the node keeps renewing it, so a dead
   machine releases its cells without a membership protocol or failure detector
   (`README.md` lines 19-22).
2. **Read-after-write consistency.** Together with the conditional create and
   conditional overwrite, this is one of three properties the object store must
   provide (`docs/guarantees.md` lines 18-24). Qualified stores are Amazon S3,
   Cloudflare R2, Tigris, Google Cloud Storage, and Azure Blob Storage; celld
   runs the release tests against R2 (`docs/guarantees.md` lines 26-28).

The ownership record names the owner's node session and carries a fencing
epoch. Every activation advances the epoch, so the replicator writes each
cell's SQLite data under `cells/<cell>/ltx/e<epoch>/`, and an epoch never has
two writers (`docs/guarantees.md` lines 108-131). A node that lost ownership
can keep writing, but its writes land in a superseded prefix.

## The clean-sheet decision core

`State` in `crates/logic/lib.rs` holds all authoritative coordination state. It
tracks each cell's `Phase`, the node authority (a lease in
`NodeAuthority`), withheld outputs behind the durability gate (`barriers`),
activation and capacity admission queues, the shedding latch, and the current
application generation.

The core never reads a clock: "the core never asks what time it is, it
remembers what it was told" (`crates/logic/lib.rs` lines 591-599). Authority is
evaluated at ask time against the published lease expiry on the remembered
monotonic clock, not by trusting a timer to have fired
(`crates/logic/lib.rs` lines 714-737). This is what lets a suspended VM still
refuse a request after resume.

The `celld-logic` crate deliberately has no I/O so that "the clock, the
randomness, and the object store are interfaces, and a simulator drives the
core" (`docs/testing.md` lines 88-95). The simulated store injects latency,
compare-and-swap races, and lost responses.

### Cell phases

The `Phase` enum (lines 113-190) enumerates the state a single cell crosses:
`Inactive`, cold-activation queuing (`WaitingActivation`), owner/lease reads
(`ReadingOwner`, `ReadingNodeLease`), the lease-fold recovery interlock
(`RecoveringOwnerLog`), capacity admission (`ReadingCapacity`,
`WaitingCapacity`), the conditional claim (`Acquiring`,
`ReconcilingAcquire`), restore (`Restoring`), runtime start/publish
(`Starting`, `Publishing`), durability proof (`EnsuringDurability`), stop
(`Cleaning`), `Dormant`, successor handoff (`Adopting`), `Resident`, and
`Remote` (cell owned by another node) and the terminal `Fenced`. The funnel
`phase_name` maps these onto stable report strings that `/state` and
`celld diagnose` publish (`crates/logic/lib.rs` lines 212-240).

### Admission and fairness

Two FIFO queues bound concurrency. `activation_waiters` bounds cold-cell
activation to `max_activations`, and `capacity_waiters` bounds residency to
`max_resident`. The capacity waiters are FIFO deliberately: "waking every
waiter on a release and letting them race is unfair by construction — under
sustained eviction a waiter can time out while thousands of slots are freed
around it", and a queue converts "eventually, probably" into a bound
(`crates/logic/lib.rs` lines 539-545). The same rationale applies to the
activation waiters.

## The actor serialization model

The executable runs one serial actor as "the only caller of
`celld_logic::on_event`" (`crates/celld/lib.rs` lines 7-10). Adapter futures
never borrow core state; they send versioned completion events back through the
actor mailbox and the actor re-enters `on_event`.

`main.rs` states the shape explicitly (lines 9-13): "One actor serializes every
event through `celld-logic`; the actor polls its mailbox, timers, and in-flight
effect futures together. This is the execution shape required for monotonic
lease ticks to fence the node even when a storage operation remains hung,
without spawning a task per effect."

The `actor` module owns the shared timer discipline via `TimerSlots` and the
`TimerSlot` enum, which keys deadlines by operation and queued activations by
cell/generation so one arming cannot silently cancel another
(`crates/celld/actor.rs` lines 39-68).

### Events and effects

The control loop is a closed circuit: the core emits an `Effect` describing an
I/O or runtime intent; the effect adapter performs it without touching `State`;
and the adapter sends back a versioned `Event` describing the outcome, which
the core consumes to advance `State`. Because `State` only ever advances
through `on_event`, every transition is replayable by the deterministic
simulator.

Fenced or lagged runtime operations are not silently dropped. The core keeps
`retired_runtime_ops` so that "Start/publish effects invalidated by fencing may
still commit. Their late completion must trigger compensating cleanup, not be
ignored" (`crates/logic/lib.rs` lines 567-569). Runtime starts that exceed
their deadline but still own a live executor task are tracked in
`timed_out_runtime_starts`, because a start cannot be cancelled safely and the
core keeps its phase until the real completion arrives (lines 574-576).

## The output gate

Every egress that can reveal a cell's state passes through one choke point —
the output gate — which withholds a response until every write it can reveal is
proven durable (`crates/logic/output_gate.rs`). This is the RPO=0 guarantee:
"celld does not answer a write until the data survives a failure"
(`docs/guarantees.md`). The gate holds each response behind a `Barrier`, and a
fence drains the gate to a failed response so a write is never acknowledged
after the node loses authority (`crates/logic/lib.rs` lines 513-522).

## Upstream and downstream relationships

- **Upstream of the core:** the network listeners (public Worker ingress,
  internal peer/operator listener), the V8 runtime, and the object-store
  client all feed `Event`s into the actor.
- **Downstream of the core:** `Effect`s drive cell activation/stop, durability
  proofs, ownership CASes, peer forwarding, and telemetry.
- **Replication and storage:** `crates/celld` wires `celld-ltx` (the
  per-cell `Db`) to the shared object-store client, laid out as
  `cells/<cell>/ltx/e<epoch>/` in the bucket (`crates/celld/ltx_repl.rs`).

## Configuration and failure behavior

Configuration surfaces as environment variables and command-line flags, and is
parsed strictly: "An unset variable selectives its documented default. A
supplied variable must contain a valid value, so a typo cannot silently change
the configuration of a running node" (`crates/celld/env_vars.rs`). A
validation pass exits at startup on a malformed value.

Failure modes center on the lease and the fencing epoch: a node that cannot
renew its lease or whose record was replaced fences itself and exits code 3
(`docs/guarantees.md` lines 200-228). The failure of a node is treated as a
normal input rather than a recovery procedure.

claims.statement: The workspace is a clean-sheet split: crates/logic owns all behavioral state and decisions as a pure decision core with no async, I/O, clocks, randomness, or locks, while crates/celld is only an effect executor and adapter host.

crates/celld is the executable that embeds V8, runs HTTP and peer listeners, owns SQLite files and the object-store client, and runs one serial actor which is the only caller of celld_logic::on_event.
A cell is a Durable Object: a named server with its own private SQLite database, and cells share no database.
The fleet bucket is the root of authority: it stores the deployments, the cell state, the ownership records, the node leases, and the peer-authentication secret.
A node claims a cell by a conditional bucket write, so the object store decides who wins and two nodes cannot both claim the same cell; the claim expires unless renewed.

The ownership record names the owner node's session and carries a fencing epoch; every activation advances the epoch徒 and the replicator writes each cell's SQLite data under cells/<cell>/ltx/e<epoch>/, so an epoch never has two writers.

The object store must provide a conditional create, a conditional overwrite, and read-after-write consistency; qualified stores are Amazon S3, Cloudflare R2, Tigris, Google Cloud Storage, and Azure Blob Storage.

crates/celld runs one serial actor that serializes every event through celld_logic::on_event and polls its mailbox, timers, and in-flight effect futures together, so monotonic lease ticks can fence the node even when a storage operation remains hung.

The core never reads a clock: it remembers what it was told through events, and node authority is evaluated at ask time against the published lease expiry on the monotonic clock rather than by trusting a timer to have fired.

celld-logic has no I/O so that the clock, the randomness, and the object store are interfaces and a deterministic simulator can drive the core, injecting latency, compare-and-swap races, and lost responses.
The output gate is one choke point every egress passes through, and it withholds a response until every write it can reveal is proven durable, which is the RPO=0 guarantee.
Fenced or lagged runtime operations are tracked by the core (retired_runtime_ops and timed_out_runtime_starts) so their late completion triggers compensating cleanup rather than being ignored.
Capacity and activation admission are FIFO queues that convert eventual fairness into a bound, preventing starvation under sustained eviction.
Configuration is parsed strictly: an unset variable selects its documented defaulteb and the process exits during startup when a supplied value is invalid.
The release profile is size-tuned with fat LTO, opt-level s, panic=abort, and strip, and the binary uses jemalloc because glibc arena serialization measured lower throughput.
